title: Quantum Computing's Next Scaling Challenge Isn't Just Qubits. It's Power. - HPCwire
html:
As I prepare to attend my 28th SC conference, I’m reminded of a lesson the high-performance computing (HPC) community has learned repeatedly: scientific breakthroughs must operate within the constraints of the infrastructure available to support them. From massively parallel supercomputers to GPU-accelerated systems and today’s AI infrastructure, we’ve continually pushed computational boundaries while confronting the realities of power, cooling and physical space limitations.

As we race towards achieving fault-tolerant quantum computing systems, most of the questions I’m answering focus on: “What scientific problems will they be able to solve?” “How reliably will they operate?” and “When will a full system actually become available?”

There’s another pressing question that cannot be ignored: Will tomorrow’s million+ qubit quantum computers fit within the existing data center environment?

While big AI data centers can contract energy at a gigawatt scale and space by the acre, HPC data centers have long been limited by both physical space and available energy. With the increased density of recent GPUs, this has evolved into energy, cooling and load-bearing capacity. Many recent meetings have begun with “we have 4 megawatts, how much of your hardware will fit in that envelope?”

The Quantum Energy Challenge

Electricity has become one of the biggest concerns and political issues in the data center business. According to the International Energy Agency, electricity demand from AI-focused data centers grew 50% in 2025, and total data center consumption is on track to nearly double to 950 TWh by 2030. Utilities, regulators and local communities are asking harder questions about grid capacity, rising power prices and the cost of the new generation and transmission needed to keep up.

That’s the environment quantum computing must integrate into.

A peer-reviewed study published in June 2026 in Renewable and Sustainable Energy Transition modeled the energy and resource needs of future fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computers, up to systems with millions of physical qubits. In one configuration, a machine with roughly 2 million physical qubits could draw 27 megawatts. Run around the clock, that’s about 237 gigawatt-hours a year, or about $27 million in electricity using the $1 Million per Megawatt rule of thumb. Now picture a center that wants more than one. Four of those machines would need about 108 megawatts of continuous power and close to a terawatt-hour a year, and that’s before counting the classical HPC systems sitting next to them.

The same study also modeled a very different outcome. With more optimistic assumptions about technology advancements, a system with ~10 million physical qubits could run on 4 megawatts. That’s five times the qubits for less than one-sixth of the power.

These are modeled scenarios, not measurements from commercial systems, and the gap between them comes down to assumptions about cryogenics, control electronics and overall system efficiency. They show that power doesn’t have to grow in lockstep with qubit count. The reality is that the design choices we make now will determine whether these machines end up as useful tools or as new burdens on the grid.

A Quantum Computer Worth Building: Millions of qubits on a single chip

At this year’s Quantum World Congress, Quantum Motion CEO James Palles-Dimmock argued that quantum computing shouldn’t reinvent manufacturing when the semiconductor industry has already spent decades learning to make billions of tiny devices. Chipmakers have been refining lithography, process control, transistor density and high-volume production for more than 50 years. That’s a strong starting point for building quantum systems with millions of physical qubits.

And that is the big reason I find the silicon-spin modality so interesting: With millions of qubits on a single chip, an entire multi-million qubit system will be able to fit in just a few standard racks and use well under a megawatt of power mostly for cooling, error correction hardware and other processes). This will eliminate the complexities associated with multiple fridge setups, networking or distributed programming.

Implicit in the single-chip design is the ability to move control electronics closer to the qubits, with multiplexing and standard CMOS techniques creating an infrastructure that is simpler, smaller, cheaper and easier, saving valuable space and energy.

Quantum Motion’s full-stack CMOS quantum computer, which was delivered to the UK’s National Quantum Computing Centre (NQCC) in 2025, shows what’s possible when a system is built around a conventional data center form factor. The broader lesson is to design the whole system for integration and power consumption needs from day one.

The HPC Community Must Help Define the Metrics

Our community has spent decades trading off performance against power. The Green500 helped make performance-per-watt a standard way to measure progress in supercomputing. The Energy Efficient High Performance Working Group (EEHPC) work that Natalie Bates has headed up for well over a decade has resulted in standards and language put into procurement requirements worldwide. Quantum computing needs the same kind of accountability, with benchmarks suited to a very different kind of machine.

Manufacturability, qubit density, deployment complexity and data center impact all need to be part of how we evaluate these systems. Quantum computers will be one more resource in heterogeneous centers, sitting alongside CPUs, GPUs and other accelerators. They can’t be stand-alone installations that each need their own new substation. The goal is to deliver useful quantum computing that fits within the power, cooling and operating envelope of a modern HPC data center.

Building Quantum Computing That HPC Can Sustain

Quantum computing has tremendous potential for advancing materials science, chemistry and other industries.

At SC26, I’m looking forward to digging into the hard question: Can a million-qubit system run within the power budgets HPC centers already have? Can semiconductor manufacturing and integrated control break the link between qubit count and energy use? How should we measure the full energy cost of a useful quantum computation? Are we building quantum computers for the data centers we have, or are we expecting data centers to rebuild around them?

We can’t wait for full-scale systems to show up before we raise these questions. The time to establish energy-efficient design principles and meaningful infrastructure benchmarks is now.

About the author:

Brent Gorda is a senior HPC industry luminary with extensive experience in parallel and distributed computing. He spent a majority of his career working in and around the U.S. Department of Energy Laboratories and providing technical consulting for startups in computing, networking and storage.
